problem: Given the function $f(x)=\frac{{x}^{2}+1}{{e}^{x}},$ which of the following statements are true?

choices.value: There is a local maximum at $x=-1$

feedback.problem: Given the function $f(x)=\frac{{x}^{2}-3x+3}{{x}^{3}}$ defined for $x\in (0,\infty ),$ which of the following statements are true?
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we find the stationary points. Differentiating $f(x)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{(2x-3){x}^{3}-3({x}^{2}-3x+3){x}^{2}}{{x}^{6}} \\  & =\frac{2{x}^{2}-3x-3{x}^{2}+9x-9}{{x}^{4}} \\  & =\frac{-{x}^{2}+6x-9}{{x}^{4}} \\  & =-\frac{(x-3)^{2}}{{x}^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving ${f}^{′}(x)=0$ gives

$$
-\frac{(x-3)^{2}}{{x}^{4}}\,⟹\,x=3.
$$

So, $x=3$ is the only stationary point of $f(x)$ on $(0,\infty ).$ Next, to determine whether this point is a local maximum or minimum, we use the first derivative test.

Let's choose the test points $x=1,4$ and evaluate the first derivative at these points.

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(1) & =-\frac{(1-3)^{2}}{{1}^{4}}=-4<0 \\ {f}^{′}(4) & =-\frac{(4-3)^{2}}{{4}^{4}}=-\frac{1}{256}<0\end{aligned}
$$

We summarize the information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $(0,3)$ | $3$ | $(3,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $1$ |  | $4$ |
| ${f}^{′}$ | $-$ | $0$ | $-$ |
| $f$ | $↘$ |  | $↘$ |

The first derivative does not change sign at $x=3.$ Therefore, we conclude that $x=3$ is neither a minimum nor a maximum.

Therefore, the first derivative test shows that the function has no local extrema on $(0,\infty ).$

submitted_fields.submitted_value: The function $f(x)$ has no local extrema
